blocks.text: Design a music streaming platform like Spotify, letting listeners stream tracks instantly from a catalog of tens of millions of songs, download tracks for offline listening, and accurately, fairly counting which plays actually qualify as a genuine, royalty-payable stream. This category's other designs already cover video transcoding and CDN delivery in depth, so this design centers on what is genuinely distinct about music streaming: a play only becomes real money owed to an artist once it meets a genuine minimum listening threshold, and a rapid, repeated restart of the same track must never be allowed to multiply that payout.

blocks.alt: A completed listen only counts as a billable stream if it met the minimum qualifying duration and was not a rapid, repeated replay of the same track by the same listener

blocks.text: The technique that makes royalty accounting both fair and fraud-resistant is a two-part qualification check on every completed listen, a minimum listen-duration threshold, and a per-listener, per-track cooldown window between counted plays, so a genuine, meaningful listen counts exactly once, while a quick skip or a rapid, repeated restart does not inflate what an artist is actually owed.

blocks.text: A listener should be able to search for and instantly play any track in the catalog. A listener should be able to download tracks for offline listening, playable without a network connection for a limited time. A completed listen should be evaluated against a minimum qualifying duration before counting toward a track's royalty-payable stream count. A rapid, repeated replay of the same track by the same listener within a short window should not count as an additional billable stream.

blocks.alt: Fair, fraud-resistant royalty accounting, reliable offline playback, instant playback start, massive concurrent streaming volume, and licensed content protection

blocks.text: Fair, fraud-resistant royalty accounting means a rapid, repeated restart of the same track must never be allowed to multiply what an artist is actually paid for it. Reliable offline playback means downloaded music should keep working without a network connection, but only within real, enforced limits tied to an active subscription. Instant playback start means tapping play has to begin audio almost immediately, never with a visible, frustrating delay. Massive concurrent streaming volume means the platform serves millions of simultaneous streams across a catalog of tens of millions of tracks. And licensed content protection means downloaded, offline content must stay tied to a genuine, currently active subscription, not become permanently, freely usable the moment it is downloaded.

blocks.text: A listener's playback request is served through the playback service and an audio CDN, while a play tracker records each session's actual listen duration. Once a session ends, a royalty qualification engine checks that duration against the minimum threshold and the listener's own recent play history for that track before recording it in the royalty ledger. Separately, downloading a track for offline listening issues a time-limited license that must be periodically refreshed while the listener remains online and subscribed.

class StreamCounter:
    # Decides whether a completed listen counts as a billable, royalty-qualifying
    # stream: it must meet a minimum listen duration, and must not be a rapid
    # repeat of the same track by the same user within an anti-abuse cooldown window.
    def __init__(self, min_qualifying_seconds, cooldown_seconds):
        self.min_qualifying_seconds = min_qualifying_seconds
        self.cooldown_seconds = cooldown_seconds
        self.last_counted_play_at = {}  # "user:track" -> last counted play time
        self.qualifying_stream_count_value = 0

    def record_play(self, user_id, track_id, started_at, listen_duration_seconds):
        if listen_duration_seconds < self.min_qualifying_seconds:
            return False  # too short to ever qualify as a billable stream, regardless of cooldown

        key = f"{user_id}:{track_id}"
        last_counted = self.last_counted_play_at.get(key)
        if last_counted is not None and (started_at - last_counted) < self.cooldown_seconds:
            return False  # meets duration, but too soon after this same user's last counted play of this track

        self.last_counted_play_at[key] = started_at  # record this as the new last counted play for this user and track
        self.qualifying_stream_count_value += 1
        return True

    def qualifying_stream_count(self):
        return self.qualifying_stream_count_value


def main():
    counter = StreamCounter(30, 120)  # 30s minimum duration, 120s anti-abuse cooldown

    # User U's first, genuine full listen of track T at time 0, 45 seconds long: qualifies, no prior play.
    print("U plays T at t=0 for 45s:", counter.record_play("U", "T", 0, 45))

    # User U replays T at t=60 (only 60s after the last counted play) for 40s: meets duration, but within cooldown.
    print("U plays T at t=60 for 40s (too soon):", counter.record_play("U", "T", 60, 40))

    # User U replays T at t=200 (200s after the last COUNTED play at t=0, past the 120s cooldown) for 35s: counted.
    print("U plays T at t=200 for 35s (cooldown passed):", counter.record_play("U", "T", 200, 35))

    # User U skips T at t=250 after only 10 seconds: never counted, regardless of cooldown.
    print("U plays T at t=250 for 10s (too short):", counter.record_play("U", "T", 250, 10))

    # A different user V plays the same track T at t=5 for 40s: evaluated entirely independently of U.
    print("V plays T at t=5 for 40s (different user):", counter.record_play("V", "T", 5, 40))

    print("Total qualifying, billable streams:", counter.qualifying_stream_count())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

items: Architecture: CDN-delivered playback feeding a play tracker and royalty qualification engine, with offline downloads governed by a separately refreshable, time-limited license.
Capacity: tens of millions of tracks, millions of concurrent streams at peak, and audio's dramatically smaller file size compared to video.
The core technique: royalty-qualifying stream counting, minimum listen duration plus an anti-abuse cooldown, worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.
Database: a listener-partitioned, append-heavy play event and royalty ledger store, alongside a small, expiry-tracked offline license store.
End-to-end workflows: a normal play-and-qualify flow and an offline license refresh flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: immediate, responsive playback entirely independent of royalty accounting timing, with royalty counts reconciled over a full period rather than required to be instantly exact.

Trade-offs: minimum duration plus per-user-per-track cooldown versus counting every play start versus requiring a full, complete listen, compared directly on fraud resistance and fairness for genuine listens.
